promo-look-colour.title: Canva hides the print colour setting behind Pro #shorts
promo-look-colour.description:
Screens make colour with light, printers make it with ink, and they cannot reach the same colours. Canva's PDF Print export offers an RGB or CMYK choice — but the same help page lists CMYK colour profile options among the features restricted to Pro. On a free plan your print file leaves in RGB and the print shop's software decides what your brand colours become. Neon orange, electric blue and lime collapse. Deep teal, burgundy and charcoal barely move.

Full tutorial and the £4.99 Lookbook Kit: https://geniusjunkie.net/lookbook-kit/

promo-look-bleed.title: The free Canva checkbox that stops the white line #shorts
promo-look-bleed.description:
A guillotine is accurate to about a millimetre. One millimetre of drift on a page with a coloured background leaves a thin white stripe down the edge — and it is not the printer being careless. Run your background past the edge of the canvas and tick Crop marks and bleed at download. Unlike the colour profile, this one is free on any plan.

Full tutorial and the £4.99 Lookbook Kit: https://geniusjunkie.net/lookbook-kit/

promo-look-dpi.title: Your photos will print soft — the 5-second check #shorts
promo-look-dpi.description:
▶️ FULL TUTORIAL: https://youtu.be/9M9z_fbDVFQ

Print renders at 300 dots per inch, roughly four times the detail a screen needs. So a photo that looks perfect in the Canva editor can print soft, and you do not find out until the box arrives.

The check takes five seconds per image: zoom the editor to 100% and look at the photo at actual size. If it is soft there, it is worse on paper.

Shooting the products yourself? Shoot bigger than you think — you can always throw pixels away. Using supplied images? Ask for the print versions, not the ones off the website. And never scale a small photo up to fill a page: enlarging does not add detail, it just makes the softness bigger.

promo-look-proof.title: Every print shop offers this — almost nobody asks #shorts
promo-look-proof.description:
▶️ FULL TUTORIAL: https://youtu.be/9M9z_fbDVFQ

Before a print shop runs fifty copies, ask one question: can I see a proof?

A proof is a single printed copy before the full run. It costs a little, and it is the only way to see the actual colour on the actual paper before you have paid for the whole job. Screens make colour with light and printers make it with ink — they cannot reach the same colours, and a proof is where you find that out cheaply instead of expensively.

Every print shop offers this. Almost nobody asks.
